articleTitle: A theory of C/sup 2/ organizations
publicationTitle: International Conference on Information-Decision-Action Systems in Complex Organisations, 1992.
abstract: The study described presents an approach to studying the assessing C/sup 2/ organizations. Command systems are considered as organizational structures which adapt themselves to variations in the availability, quality, quantity and timeliness of received information, and in response to the availability and performance of communication links and other resources. The authors present a derived theory of C/sup 2/ organizations, particularly applying the work of the management theorists J.R. Galbraith (1974) and H. Mintzberg (1979). This provides an integrated set of principles for assessing and studying C/sup 2/ organizations. This should enable C/sup 2/ organizations to be assessed from an organizational perspective, thus giving the human parts of the system due consideration. It provides a means to understand how organizations work, how different task distributions affect performance and how different team groupings and structures affect performance.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An expert system to assist operators of the power system control centres
publicationTitle: International Conference on Information-Decision-Action Systems in Complex Organisations, 1992.
abstract: Discusses the interaction between the information system and the operators in power system control centres. This interaction is not very easy in the systems in use, because they do not take into account human limitations. The authors present an expert system that gives special importance to dialogue with the operators. The graphic interface is very interactive, being based on a system with windows and buttons. The expert system presented is a good decision-support tool, providing the operators with an intelligent analysis of the available information. The expert system works on real alarm lists received at the Portuguese control centres.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Decision support for energy management systems
publicationTitle: International Conference on Information-Decision-Action Systems in Complex Organisations, 1992.
abstract: Operating a power network is a difficult task because a power network is a dynamic, changing system functioning in a dynamic, changing environment. Operators use energy management systems (EMS) to help them operate the network, but finally the control of power networks is still based on the intervention of operators. With ever-increasing system complexity, operators clearly require more sophisticated assistance, i.e., the need for more formalized decision support in EMS. The only way to reduce the complexity of operating in any general and substantial way is to integrate decision support with the whole operating process. The authors' research adopts a large-scale approach in order to achieve this. They first explore the issues associated with operating. They then consider the need for decision support and discuss proposals for a decision support framework. The key aspect to the research is making the available but non-homogeneous information easily accessible to the operator by using knowledge-based and object-oriented techniques.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Analysis of aircrew decision-making
publicationTitle: International Conference on Information-Decision-Action Systems in Complex Organisations, 1992.
abstract: A study of aircrew behaviour and work-load was carried out as part of the MOD Defence Research Agency (Aerospace Division) Advanced Panoramic Helmet-mounted Integrated Display System (APHIDS) programme; this programme has the aim of conducting research into the design and evaluation of advanced display systems for future combat aircraft. The initial study was concerned with the design of an experimental system, which would be used to explore various display options and examine their impact on aircrew performance. It was considered important that the design of the experimental system should be based on an accurate and detailed model of aircrew behaviour and requirements; in consequence, the adaptive decision-maker (ADM) model was selected to provide a formalism for representing aircrew expertise and estimating work-load and information requirements. Application of this model provided a basis for exploring the factors contributing to aircrew work-load, for identifying opportunities for the use of advanced display systems to reduce the work-load, and for estimating the potential reduction in work-load. The authors describe the approach used in developing the model of aircrew behaviour, outline the work-load analysis and discuss some of the conclusions reached in the analysis.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Comparing decision aids for technology transfers
publicationTitle: International Conference on Information-Decision-Action Systems in Complex Organisations, 1992.
abstract: Proponents of various decision aid systems loudly proclaim the merits of 'their' system over all competition, especially 'brand X,' and justify their own process because it does a 'better job of decision making' than that done by competing products. In order to compare such decision aids independently, a systematic process was conceived, designed, constructed, tested and implemented. The purpose was to use automation to standardize a decision process among diverse adversaries in a dynamic, complex, technological environment. The process first step structured the factors needed to arrive at an equitable decision on technology transfer from domestic to foreign ownership, control, or influence. The factors were identified by participants in the decentralized decision process. Using group problem solving techniques, the most important factors were identified and ranked. Factor weights were determined with automated aids. Four decision processes were evaluated to determine their accuracy in arriving at a decision dealing with proposed technology transfers. The author deals with the process of identifying the factors and testing the decision aids.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Database synchronisation in military command and control systems
publicationTitle: International Conference on Information-Decision-Action Systems in Complex Organisations, 1992.
abstract: Database synchronisation is a vital aspect of any database system, be it commercial or military. It is especially important in military C/sup 3/I systems where critical decisions may be taken as a result of database information. Database synchronisation means that the data viewed by one user must be the same as that viewed by another user at a different physical location or node. This meas that the database system must maintain not only local integrity but also global consistency across all nodes. This is a complex task given the communications problems specific to military C/sup 3/I systems. Database synchronisation in military C/sup 3/I systems is a critical issue that is not fully addressed by the commercial database products currently available. With few exceptions, military customers need bespoke database software that can be specifically tailored to their precise requirements.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A fully-featured human computer interface for intelligence and command and control applications
publicationTitle: International Conference on Information-Decision-Action Systems in Complex Organisations, 1992.
abstract: The Intelligence Workstation Human Computer Interface (IW/HCI) represents an exciting new development in the field of human-computer interfaces for information- decision-action systems. It offers a graphical user interface with a consistent look and feel across software applications, an intuitive method of operation, a sophisticated information exchange mechanism and comprehensive database access features. In addition, it utilises the emerging open system software standards for machine-independent operation. The IW/HCI has been specifically designed for the demanding requirements of military command-information-systems. However, it is also seen to be applicable to a wide range of systems which require historically traceable decisions and actions to be made on the basis of highly dynamic and incomplete information.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Alternative views of the quality of military plans
publicationTitle: International Conference on Information-Decision-Action Systems in Complex Organisations, 1992.
abstract: Two types of military plan are characterised; off-load plans (that concern the off-load of men and equipment during amphibious operations) and SSGW plans (plans for attack with surface-to-surface guided weapons). The selection of these types of plan was largely determined by pragmatic considerations, such as access to users. Current practice views of their quality are presented. Then, some general knowledge of the domain of military plans is outlined and alternative views of these plans are proposed. Finally, the current practice and alternative views of plan quality are compared and contrasted.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A mission oriented approach to system development
publicationTitle: International Conference on Information-Decision-Action Systems in Complex Organisations, 1992.
abstract: The systems under consideration are information-decision- action systems in complex organizations. This paper is concerned with the purpose and functioning of action systems in such organizations but excludes organizations, however complex, which exist for spiritual or unmeasurable political objectives. The information-decision element is covered briefly. One of many methods of analyzing the functioning of a organization is known as a mission oriented approach (MOA). The advantage of MOA is that it provides a framework to plan system improvements or new systems in a way which keeps the overriding strategy and major tasks or missions required to support that strategy in mind. In the context of information-decision-action systems in complex organizations MOA can be used to analyze very complicated systems. The structure, by keeping strictly to the performance of an act or series of actions, steers clear of preconceived solutions until all solutions can be considered. This provides a bridge between the strategists, managers, scientists, technologists, operators, analysts and those who provide support.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An engineering view of the human interface
publicationTitle: International Conference on Information-Decision-Action Systems in Complex Organisations, 1992.
abstract: An examination is given of the human half of the human computer interface (HCI) from an engineering viewpoint. Humans are complex systems in their own right which would take many years to understand, but there are groups who have provided a relatively simple model for the analysis of humans and their transactions. The model and methodology is transactional analysis (TA) as proposed by E. Berne (1972). TA is the study of human interaction by the study of people's ego states and the communications between states, both internally and externally. The ego states defined are: parent (defining those elements learnt from authority figures); adult (defining those elements which are processed and considered); and child (defining those elements concerned with emotion, charm and creativity). The three ego states are present in every person and one's actions can be interpreted as resulting from one or other of these states.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Methods for assessing tactical decisionmaking in battle
publicationTitle: International Conference on Information-Decision-Action Systems in Complex Organisations, 1992.
abstract: A method is described for assessing military command decisionmaking using simulation experiments and dynamic simulation modelling, along with some typical results. The simulation studies have been carried out in the Research, Engineering, and Systems Analysis (RESA) facility. RESA is a facility for presenting large-scale, event-driven battle simulations with realistic scenarios. The RESA facility has been used primarily for training naval battle force staffs and for studies of advanced sensor and weapons concepts. The author's interest was to use the RESA facility for man-in-the-loop studies to determine the cognitive and decision processes of warfare commanders during battle. The simulation experiments measured the overall effectiveness of the C/sup 3/I system with the performance of the commanders as its principal determining factor. The aim of the research program is to improve the design of future C/sup 3/I systems by identifying and ameliorating human information processing and decisionmaking problems associated with critical battle decisions.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Successful implementation of a knowledge based, smelter operations scheduling system at the Palabora Mine in South Africa
publicationTitle: International Conference on Information-Decision-Action Systems in Complex Organisations, 1992.
abstract: Summarises work done by RTZ's ITSU in applying knowledge based technology to the management of a copper smelter, and the SCHEDEX system that evolved from this. Particular emphasis is given to the way in which the technology was introduced into the operations environment, the benefits of using a participative approach and 'soft systems' perspective in the analysis and design process, and the necessity of understanding the issues within a holistic context. Development and implementation of SCHEDEX was not problem-free, but provided some valuable learning experiences which can be built on in the future.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A realistic simulation of human decision making behaviour
publicationTitle: International Conference on Information-Decision-Action Systems in Complex Organisations, 1992.
abstract: A description is given of a two-year-project to build a realistic computer model of a human decision maker in naval combat situations. The area of focus is anti air warfare (AAW). The threat from air attack poses one of the greatest risks to ship safety. The approach of the study is to focus on an individual within the AAW team and create a computer model to be integrated with the existing combat model. The individual being modelled is the anti air warfare officer (AAWO), the senior air defence officer on the Royal Navy Type 42 Destroyer. The Type 42 is the primary air defence ship in the Royal Navy. The decision making model is an enhancement of an existing combat model, and is to be used for equipment effectiveness, tactical procedures and command and control studies. Previously, in such combat models, the role of the human decision maker has had to be simplified or ignored, yet he may be the greatest source of variability or uncertainty. This project is attempting to redress this imbalance.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The on-line vehicle scheduler
publicationTitle: International Conference on Information-Decision-Action Systems in Complex Organisations, 1992.
abstract: Software developed by the author to support the task of online interactive vehicle scheduling is described. This software has been designed to meet the needs of 'Dial-a-Ride' operations. They develop vehicle schedules interactively to meet users needs which are received over the telephone. The software is operational at Tyne and Wear PTE and an enhanced version is used by Merseyside PTE. The author gives details of the human computer interface which is used and explains the choice of programming language operating system platform. The author continues with the proposed solution to a wider problem-computerised interactive vehicle scheduling for large (>50) vehicle fleets. This solution is based on multi-dimensional indexing techniques.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Modelling organisational complexity using the ORDIT framework
publicationTitle: International Conference on Information-Decision-Action Systems in Complex Organisations, 1992.
abstract: ORDIT (Organisational Requirements Definition for Information Technology) is a five year project (ESPRIT Project No 2301) which includes collaborators from both industry and academia. The ORDIT project has the objective of creating a practical design methodology and supporting tools which will enable those engaged in systems analysis and design to consider in detail the human requirements of complex socio-technical systems. The authors provide an overview of this methodology the design infrastructure and focus on describing the notation being developed and highlighting what it has to offer the IT designer.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: SSM as an aid to requirements definition
publicationTitle: International Conference on Information-Decision-Action Systems in Complex Organisations, 1992.
abstract: A discussion is given on how soft systems methodology (SSM) can aid requirements definition in a complex organisation. The discussion is illustrated with examples from the army's command, control and communication information system (CIS) programme. Whether requirements definition is a problem in a complex organisation depends on where in that organisation you are. In the army, if one tells a Royal Artillery officer to 'get a better 155 mm howitzer' the production of a statement of operational requirement (OR) is not too difficult. But ask a member of the army resources and plans staff to approve that 155 mm howitzer requirement when it is in contention for funding with an improved CIS and it is likely that the relative cost effectiveness of both will be scrutinised much more fully than they would have been if not in contention for funds and probably their ORs subjected to considerable revision. It is this interplay of technical aspiration with the constraints of available funding which makes the task of producing an OR so difficult. Nowhere in the army is this more so than in the CIS area. The author focuses specifically on CIS, but many of the principles which are discussed apply across the board of requirements definition work.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Towards an analysis and specification method for IDA systems
publicationTitle: International Conference on Information-Decision-Action Systems in Complex Organisations, 1992.
abstract: The management of the software development process is made difficult by the creative nature of design. The design of a system is really a process of discovery, both by the user and the developer. This is what causes the requirements to evolve and it also means that the system developer is most likely to be in a position to propose the best design just when too many decisions have been taken and it is already too late. This paper explains the various types and sources of complexity inherent in IDA systems and proposes an analysis and specification framework within which they can be addressed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An ODP model for military IDA systems (open distributed processing)
publicationTitle: International Conference on Information-Decision-Action Systems in Complex Organisations, 1992.
abstract: Modern warfare requires fast, reliable support from logistic systems. Sophisticated high technology weapons demand fast reaction on the battlefield. This leads to a greater need for automation and interoperation of computer systems, from sensing, through action, to support systems. This paper suggests how interoperability within military command, control, communications and information (C3I) systems can be analysed and ultimately could be achieved. This paper presents chosen results of MoD sponsored research within the Methods of C3I Interoperability (MCI) Programme. The primary focus is towards interoperability, but with a secondary focus on procurement. The aim is to assist the MoD to specify systems with sufficient inherent versatility for interoperation when needs arise.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: How can the user get what he want? (Command support systems)
publicationTitle: International Conference on Information-Decision-Action Systems in Complex Organisations, 1992.
abstract: Some of the most complex and high risk information-decision-action systems are those demanded by the military and civil authorities as command and control information systems (CClS) or command support systems (CSS). A significant number of these systems have, in some sense, failed, due to cost overruns, late delivery and, most importantly, inability to satisfy the users' requirements. Both the common causes of user dissatisfaction and the methods currently used by the authors during system implementation to ensure user satisfaction are examined. In particular, a method of determining the requirement for automated support to meet the specific organisational and procedural needs of military and civil headquarters by the use of a command support system demonstrator (CSSD) is described. The CSSD is a state-of-the-art distributed prototyping tool.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An adaptable expert aid to fault diagnosis in satellite communication networks
publicationTitle: International Conference on Information-Decision-Action Systems in Complex Organisations, 1992.
abstract: Use of knowledge based systems as decision aids in complex environments can reduce both manpower requirements and training levels needed by system users. The Satcomms Network Expert (SaNE) is a diagnostic system intended to act as an intelligent assistant to satcomms network controllers. Its function is to reduce the sensory overload experienced during crises and periods of heavy workload. In the event of network problems, the SaNE can help an operator to focus by pre-processing the incoming alarm data and presenting suggestions as to where the network the problem might lie. The SaNE was developed using the ESB-96 expert system shell and object-oriented model building tool. The SaNE utilises aspects of a number of AI concepts including model-based causal reasoning and hierarchical knowledge bases. This paper illustrates how these innovative techniques can be incorporated into a practical, commercially oriented system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Requirements construction and the process of validation
publicationTitle: International Conference on Information-Decision-Action Systems in Complex Organisations, 1992.
abstract: Deriving, or constructing, a set of requirements for a system is a highly interactive and cooperative social process. Checking information for its perceived correctness and completeness is an important part of the specification development process and is known as validating the requirements specifications documents. This paper focuses on the method whereby the end users check the completeness and correctness of the retirements specification. User validation involves the end users of the system approving the specified system with regard to their tasks, goals and responsibilities. This method indicates whether the specification is complete and adequately supports the roles of the users. This paper is based on a case study of an experimental system which was developed to investigate how stakeholders validate the requirements specification. The results indicated that currently available formalised diagrams and concepts concerned with information processing are inappropriate for user validation. The problems which users encountered are discussed and some recommendations for addressing these are outlined.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Combat system performance modelling tools and their use
publicationTitle: International Conference on Information-Decision-Action Systems in Complex Organisations, 1992.
abstract: Discusses the area of performance tools for design assessment. This is based on complementary innovative tools which, together, provide an interactive basis for the development and assessment of system performance characteristics. The tools have been applied to combat systems, but the methodologies apply to more general areas. These combat systems are real-time systems requiring a rapid response with both operator interactions and automated responses. This paper discusses: the nature and merits of the tools; uses of the tools; and how the tools complement each other.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Integrating human factors with system development methods: an overview of a structured human factors method
publicationTitle: International Conference on Information-Decision-Action Systems in Complex Organisations, 1992.
abstract: The typical involvement of human factors (HF) only at the evaluation stage of system development often results in poor realisation of HF contributions. By emulating the characteristics of SADMs, a structured HF method that covers the system design cycle is developed. Since the method complies with the requirements of a SADM it is expected to inherit the desirable characteristics of SADMs (e.g. the benefits of systematic analysis and design). Also, by recruiting existing national schemes of SADMs, the communication of HF design products to software engineers is also facilitated. In addition, structured integration of software engineering and HF design could be achieved effectively by integrating a particular SADM with the described structure HF method. To this end, the explicit characteristics of both methods would support the identification of design inter-dependencies between the disciplines. The relevance (e.g. scope and timeliness) and applicability (e.g. format and granularity) of HF inputs with respect to the system design cycle are thus ensured. Consequently, an improved uptake of HF may be expected to accrue.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A method to ensure that IT system designs meet operational performance requirements
publicationTitle: International Conference on Information-Decision-Action Systems in Complex Organisations, 1992.
abstract: Siemens Plessey Defence Systems has been refining its approach to performance assurance. This approach has now been formalised as the 'SPDS performance modelling methodology'. This method is now supported by a graphical toolkit called the Performance Assurance Toolkit (PAT) which also provides a configuration control mechanism. This paper outlines the need for a formal performance assessment during the system design lifecycle and presents the approach developed by Siemens Plessey to address system performance. The method is well developed and fully described in Siemens Plessey documents; the paper gives a brief overview of the method along with the benefits that can be achieved through its application during system development.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Medial surface models of rational expected utility maximizing decision-making (REDM)
publicationTitle: International Conference on Information-Decision-Action Systems in Complex Organisations, 1992.
abstract: The increased complexity of modern societal, geopolitical, and military environments has stressed the need for a new understanding of nature of information-decision-action systems in order to support decision-making. Additional research into the nature of perception and how perceptions are linked into the decision-making process is also a high priority. As a contribution to these goals, catastrophe landscapes and medial surfaces, which serve as decisional landscape models of the decision-making process have been developed. Their use as models of satisficing decision-making (SDM) and rational expected utility maximization decision-making (REDM), respectively, are described and analysed. This analysis demonstrates that selection of a REDM strategy can preclude the emergence of compromise in conflicting situations that are subject to external fact-finding and arbitration.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A domain analysis of air traffic management
publicationTitle: International Conference on Information-Decision-Action Systems in Complex Organisations, 1992.
abstract: A discussion is given on the design of interactive planning support for air traffic management. Developing such support must, at the very least, take account of the controller's traditional planning tool-the flight progress strip. Indeed, consideration of development policies of evolutionary change and greater automation suggests the need for an explicitly formulation of the design problem entailed by the use of flight progress strips for planning. The article reports research which aims to produce such a formulation. Specifically, it presents an analytic characterisation of the domain of air traffic management and illustrates the reconsideration of the flight progress strip facilitated by that characterisation.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The desktop strategist: analysis of the intellectual support requirements for executives
publicationTitle: International Conference on Information-Decision-Action Systems in Complex Organisations, 1992.
abstract: The thinking executive's need for an IDAS (information decision-action system) is explained. General requirements for a desktop IDAS to support strategic executive thinking are outlined. The authors focus on one aspect only of an executive IDAS-the intellectual support requirement that should be delivered by the computer aid. This means that the support is regarded as an interactive thinking aid for what may be called the rational executive's thought-experiment process (T-E). The T-E process can be represented as a sequential state-transition process during which the thinker transits from states of uncertainty to states of increasing clarification. Each transition takes place in a distinct thought space defined in terms of a four compartment matrix for the type of entities and relationships involved: tangible or intangible for the entities; logical or deterministic for the relations.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The importance of fractal phenomena to information decision-action systems
publicationTitle: International Conference on Information-Decision-Action Systems in Complex Organisations, 1992.
abstract: The authors' experience in information decision-action systems (IDAS) is primarily with the specification, testing, and operation of large integrated military communication networks and computer systems that support military decision making. During the development cycle and under operational stress they have encountered examples of incompatibility between these IDAS and the people who use them. To understand these incompatibilities, they have taken ever broader perspectives to include the entire mission area, user organizations and non-military situations. From this perspective the authors have found that decision-makers, operators and system designers systematically underestimate the range of variation they are likely to encounter. They also found that fractal mathematics was often able to model the range of observed variation, relate the many components of these integrated processes, and clarify reasons for the persistence of incompatibilities. Their empirical work consists of analyzing real data sets for a fit to the hyperbolic distribution. When the hyperbolic distribution is found, or is expected from other related cases, the authors are often able to gain insights into the incompatibilities between users and the IDAS they employed. They discuss several examples of this. These empirical results stand on their own without reference to any underlying fractal mathematics.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Addressing operator errors in supervisory systems
publicationTitle: International Conference on Information-Decision-Action Systems in Complex Organisations, 1992.
abstract: An investigation is given of human interaction with systems in which the user takes a supervisory role. These systems include process control, power generation, command and control, military and commercial aviation and medical life-support systems. Such systems share the properties of complexity, safety-criticality and the need to operate in a time-constrained environment. They also involve the pre-processing of data before the operator is given the information. Such systems occasionally fail in dramatic ways and such failures are usually blamed on 'operator error'. However, the author argues that such failures are often due to characteristics of the system which arise as part of the engineering process and the way these characteristics are presented to the user. An analysis is given of such systems which relates the factors which may lead to operating accidents to three system components: the process under control, the human user or operator and the interface between user and process. It is proposed that by constructing the interface to present the salient task information given the behaviour of the process it is possible to reduce the complexity of the system as perceived by the user and thus reduce operating errors and improve overall system performance.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: ECOS: a configurable multi-terabyte database supporting engineering and technical computing on the Sizewell 'B' nuclear power station
publicationTitle: International Conference on Information-Decision-Action Systems in Complex Organisations, 1992.
abstract: The Sizewell 'B' PWR nuclear power station has three computing support systems: the process control, data and alarm display system; the management and administration system; and the engineering and technical support system (ECOS). In most industrial plants, only the process control and alarm handling systems support high pressure, time-critical activity. In some plants-those which must respond flexibly to market conditions-the management and administration systems must also offer such support. However, the author shows that in the complex technical environment of a nuclear power station, the engineering and technical system too is crucial, and must be designed as a component of an information-decision-action system (IDAS). The author therefore describes the role of ECOS in supporting high-pressure time-critical activities on Sizewell 'B', and explains the features of its design which enable it to fulfil this role.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The impact on the decision making process in organisations resulting from structural change in response to dynamic changing environments
publicationTitle: International Conference on Information-Decision-Action Systems in Complex Organisations, 1992.
abstract: Many organisations are changing their structure to a flat flexible profile in order to respond to dynamic changing environments. The behaviour of created task based teams is examined using a paradigm comparison approach in order to understand resultant performance and possible causes. This approach has been found to be useful in the analysis of decision making and quality.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Why the objectives of complex organisation must determine information-decision-action systems
publicationTitle: International Conference on Information-Decision-Action Systems in Complex Organisations, 1992.
abstract: A discussion is given on the influence that objectives and constraints have on decision making in an organisation and how their effect on organisation ecology can be modified by complex information-decision-action systems (IDAS). The focus of the authors is to demonstrate how the objectives and constraints can act as a filtering process on the environmental data, they in turn determine the type and evolution of organisations and then how these organisations make their decisions. How these decisions are made will govern the actions of the systems population.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Qualitative judgemental forecasting methods for use in strategic decision making
publicationTitle: International Conference on Information-Decision-Action Systems in Complex Organisations, 1992.
abstract: Forecasting, in either implicit or explicit form, is a crucial capability for information-decision-action systems operating in uncertain environments. Strategic and operational decision making may depend heavily on predictions of what the physical environment, markets, competitors or enemies will do. However, the forecasting methods which are available at present divide between quantitative techniques and qualitative methods. Since neither technique can do the job of the other, and most problem domains present a mixture of quantitative and qualitative problems, this jeopardises the creation of a coherent management and control system and produces a ragged interface between technological decision support and human decision makers. The techniques given for structuring, performing, improving, evaluating and (eventually) automating qualitative forecasting tasks, can help to address these issues in several ways: by extracting and explicating the predictive principles of the human decision maker, they provide a form of knowledge elicitation suitable for look-ahead systems in a variety of domains; they provide a basis for evaluating prototype and partial systems; they provide manual alternatives in the interim, which self-adapt, create new insights, and continually produce their own methodological enhancements for use in system design and concurrent manual decision tasks.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: JOTS-a military C3D2 core operating system and development environment for distributed decision making
publicationTitle: International Conference on Information-Decision-Action Systems in Complex Organisations, 1992.
abstract: The Joint Operational Tactical System (JOTS) II was developed to provide a highly transportable 'core' command and control system that can be used as both a functional/operational C2 system and a developmental environment for distributive, networked systems at diverse activities. Extending the metaphor of open systems architecture to command and control, JOTS II is coded on top of several layers of contractor-off-the-shelf software (UNIX, X-Windows, GUI, RDBMS, X.25, etc.) and provides a collection of inter-operating client-server applications that perform generic command and control activities, as well as a host of multi-purpose military functions. The concept enables user activities to concentrate their development in their functional mission areas rather than the underlying support C2 applications. JOTS II is a real-time networked force fusion and situation tracking system, a communications and message management system, a distributed data processing system, and an advanced tactical planning and alternatives assessment system. It incorporates modern and generic methods for data processing, display, and data distribution, as well as state-of-the-art mathematical modelling for prediction and state filtering.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: It's not easy being a customer (for software-intensive projects)
publicationTitle: International Conference on Information-Decision-Action Systems in Complex Organisations, 1992.
abstract: In operation, software-intensive projects (SIPs), particularly command, control and communications information systems are faced not only with a dynamic environment but also with a variety of situations, the nature of which cannot always be known beforehand. Requirements, therefore, are generally only an approximation of what is really needed if only the problem were better understood. This paper reviews the changes to the MOD's acquisition procedures which have recently been introduced following the categorisation of SIPs as inherently high risk projects.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: User requirements capture and specification
publicationTitle: International Conference on Information-Decision-Action Systems in Complex Organisations, 1992.
abstract: The authors identify 'poor communication of the need' as one of the significant causes of dissatisfaction in the acquisition of complex systems and consider that this stems from differing perceptions of the problem domain. The authors have outlined their approach to the development and implementation of a new method for capturing and expressing requirements and, on the basis of the work undertaken to date, they consider that it will provide a qualitative improvement over current practice. However, they can find only one test that provides quantitatively meaningful results when applied to any method, structured or otherwise, used to develop specifications. That is. did the customer consider that he got what he asked for?.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Interoperability problems-prevention is better than cure
publicationTitle: International Conference on Information-Decision-Action Systems in Complex Organisations, 1992.
abstract: For many years there has been a tendency for very large scale systems to be conceived and built as an amalgamation of a number of smaller systems. Such 'systems of systems' appear to be merely extensions of the normal engineering practice in which systems are made up of a number of sub-systems which can often operate independently to perform a complete function of some sort and so be properly defined as smaller systems in their own right. Given this, why do the large 'systems of systems' or 'supersystems' seem to produce a disproportionate number of problems when compared to their smaller counterparts? The problem in evolving the supersystem is how to integrate the component systems so that they work as a combined whole. The answer clearly lies in achieving interoperability between them, and experience is that this has very rarely been as successful as intended. The purpose of this paper is to discuss the nature of supersystems, to describe interoperability and its role in the development of such systems, and to propose a means for reducing the risk of interoperability problems occurring. The method proposed relies upon the concepts of OSI and recognises the importance and role of the operator as part of the system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Adaptive computer support in future naval systems
publicationTitle: International Conference on Information-Decision-Action Systems in Complex Organisations, 1992.
abstract: Increasing pressures to reduce manpower and improve the performance of manned systems has resulted in a shift from manpower-intensive to automation-intensive information-decision-action systems (IDAS). This trend is continuing despite the emergence of automation-induced problems for those humans who must interact with semi-automated systems. If new technologies are to achieve their full potential, then new ways must be found of improving the compatibility between these technologies and the people who must use them effectively. One approach to improving compatibility may be to develop systems which are more responsive to changing aspects of the environment such as the user and the context. Systems with these capabilities are often referred to as adaptive systems or adaptive/intelligent interfaces, etc. The prospect of developing computer systems capable of adapting to the user and the changing context, within dynamic real-time naval IDAS, is being explored at the author's agency.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Accuracy and timeliness in developing a tactical picture
publicationTitle: International Conference on Information-Decision-Action Systems in Complex Organisations, 1992.
abstract: The generation of the tactical picture for the battle group commander from data obtained from organic and non-organic sensors is the particular problem addressed to demonstrate the trade-off between accuracy and timeliness. A colored Petri net model, representing in an aggregated form the architecture for the generation of the tactical picture, is used to formulate the trade-off problem. An illustrative example is used to show the kind of analysis that can be carried out.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
